---
title: Kernel Mixture Densities
---

This page is the technical description of [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDist]] and its two
subclasses, [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKDE]] and [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistVKDE]].
These reconstruct a probability density from a set of sample points and draw from the
result. Their main use in the library is as the proposal of the APES sampler,
[[numcosmo-math|NcmFitESMCMCWalkerAPES]], where the quality of the reconstruction sets
the acceptance of the chain.

## The interpolant

For a $d$-dimensional function $g(x)$, the interpolant is

$$
s(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \phi\left(|x-x_i|, \Sigma_i\right),
\qquad x \in \mathbf{R}^d,
$$ {#eq-interpolant}

where $x_i$ are the sample points, $\Sigma_i$ sets the scale and shape of the kernel at
$x_i$, and $\lambda_i$ is its weight. The weights are chosen so that

$$
s(x_i) = g(x_i).
$$ {#eq-interp-conditions}

Evaluating the kernels at the sample points gives the interpolation matrix $\Phi$, and
the target values $g(x_i)$ give $G$, so that @eq-interp-conditions reads

$$
G = \lambda \Phi.
$$ {#eq-nnls}

This is solved as a non-negative linear least-squares problem [@LawsonHanson1974], which
keeps $\lambda_i \geq 0$. The weights are then divided by their sum, making them a
probability distribution over the kernels, and mixed with the uniform weights $1/n$ in a
fixed proportion. Sampling draws a kernel with probability $\lambda_i$, then a point
from that kernel. For an introduction to radial basis interpolation see [@DuToit2008].

The caller supplies the target as $-2\ln g(x_i)$, which is the natural form when $g$ is
a posterior.

## Center shrinkage

A kernel mixture built on the sample points is wider than the sample it came from. The
correction implemented here is the one introduced by @West1993 for mixture
approximations to posteriors, and used since in sequential Monte Carlo.

Sampling the mixture is a two-step draw: select a kernel $I$ with probability
$\lambda_I$, then draw a point from it. Write $\langle \cdot \rangle$ for the average
over that selection, and let $m_I$ and $S_I$ be the center and the covariance of the
selected kernel. The law of total covariance splits the covariance of the result $Y$
into the covariance of the centers and the mean covariance within a kernel,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Y) = \mathrm{Cov}\left(m_I\right) + \left\langle S_I \right\rangle.
$$ {#eq-total-cov}

Let $\mu$ and $C$ be the mean and the covariance of the sample points. In an ordinary
kernel density estimate the kernels sit on the sample points and each has covariance
$h^2 C$, with $h$ the bandwidth, so a draw is $Y = x_I + \varepsilon$ with
$\mathrm{Cov}(\varepsilon) = h^2 C$. The first term of @eq-total-cov is $C$ and the
second $h^2 C$,

$$
\mathrm{Cov}(Y) = C + h^2 C = \left(1 + h^2\right) C,
$$ {#eq-kde-inflation}

so the mixture is wider than the sample it is built from, by a factor that grows with
the bandwidth.

Center shrinkage removes that excess by moving the centers toward $\mu$. Placing them at

$$
c_i = \mu + a \left(x_i - \mu\right), \qquad 0 < a \leq 1,
$$ {#eq-centers}

gives them covariance $a^2 C$. Writing the kernel covariance as $b^2 C$, the two terms
of @eq-total-cov are $a^2 C$ and $b^2 C$, so the mixture reproduces $C$ when

$$
a^2 + b^2 = 1.
$$ {#eq-budget}

The centers and the kernels share one covariance budget, and $a$ trades the two against
each other while their sum stays fixed. @West1993 takes $b = h$ directly, so that
$a = \sqrt{1 - h^2}$ and the bandwidth is restricted to $h < 1$. The implementation here
instead narrows the kernels by the same factor it moves the centers, $b = a h$, which
determines both and leaves $h$ unrestricted,

$$
a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h^2}}, \qquad b = \frac{h}{\sqrt{1 + h^2}}.
$$ {#eq-a-and-b}

For $h \to 0$, $a \to 1$ and $b \to 0$: the centers stay on the sample points and this
is the narrow-kernel limit of the usual estimate. For $h \to \infty$, $a \to 0$ and
$b \to 1$: the centers collapse onto $\mu$ and each kernel carries the whole of $C$, so
the mixture becomes a single kernel centered at $\mu$ with covariance $C$.

### When the budget is exact

$\mu$ and $C$ are the mean and the covariance of the sample points, both unweighted: the
implementation takes $\mu$ as their arithmetic mean and $C$ from the same points with no
weights applied. @eq-budget therefore holds exactly when the weights $\lambda_i$ are
equal, which is the mixture prepared without interpolation. One thing makes it
approximate: with unequal weights both terms of @eq-total-cov are $\lambda$-weighted
while $\mu$ and $C$ are not. The weights that come out of @eq-nnls are not equal.

### The general transform

A fixed-bandwidth estimator with the sample covariance gives every kernel the scale
matrix $C$, and the scalar $a$ of @eq-a-and-b is exact. In general the kernel scale
matrices $\Sigma_i$ are not proportional to $C$ -- a fixed or robust covariance in
[[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKDE]], or the per-kernel $\Sigma_i$ of
[[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistVKDE]] -- and no scalar satisfies @eq-budget as a matrix
equation. The implementation contracts by a matrix instead. With

$$
c_i = \mu + A \left(x_i - \mu\right), \qquad
\Sigma_i \to \hat A \Sigma_i \hat A^T, \qquad
A = a \hat A, \quad \det \hat A = 1,
$$ {#eq-matrix-transform}

and the bandwidth in use $a h$, the two terms of @eq-total-cov are $A C A^T$ and
$\kappa h^2 A \langle\Sigma\rangle A^T$, where $\langle\Sigma\rangle$ is the mean of
the kernel scale matrices and $\kappa$ the kernel variance factor of the next section, so
the budget reads

$$
A \left(C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle\right) A^T = C.
$$ {#eq-matrix-budget}

With the Cholesky factors $C = U_C^T U_C$ and
$M = C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle = U_M^T U_M$ a solution is

$$
A = U_C^T U_M^{-T}, \qquad a = \det(A)^{1/d} = \left(\frac{\det C}{\det M}\right)^{1/2d},
$$ {#eq-matrix-solution}

two factorizations and one triangular solve. $\hat A$ has unit determinant, so it leaves
every kernel normalization unchanged. For $\langle\Sigma\rangle \propto C$ the transform
is isotropic, $A = a I$, and @eq-a-and-b is recovered; the library detects that case and
applies the scalar.

### The kernel variance factor

The covariance of a kernel need not equal the scale matrix it is parameterized by. Their
ratio $\kappa$ is $1$ for [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKernelGauss]] and $\nu/(\nu-2)$
for [[numcosmo-math|NcmStatsDistKernelST]] with $\nu$ degrees of freedom; it is the
factor in front of $h^2$ in @eq-matrix-budget. Center shrinkage needs a kernel with a
finite covariance, since $\kappa$ has to exist. The Student-t kernel with $\nu \leq 2$,
the Cauchy kernel included, has none and is refused. The sample points $x_i$ remain the
points at which the conditions @eq-interp-conditions are imposed; only the kernels move
and change shape.

## Automatic kernel selection

The bandwidth can be fitted by cross-validation, holding out part of the sample and
maximizing the held-out likelihood of the reconstruction. The same objective can choose
the kernel, by treating the Student-t degrees of freedom $\nu$ as a second fitted
parameter alongside $h$: the fit runs over $(\ln h, \ln \nu)$, and $\nu \to \infty$
recovers the Gaussian kernel, which is installed as one when the fit reaches the top of
the range. The tail weight of the kernel then follows the tail weight of the target
instead of being fixed by the caller.

Center shrinkage is not fitted. The held-out objective is a Kullback-Leibler criterion,
and $\mathrm{KL}(\pi \,\|\, \tilde p)$ penalizes a proposal that is too narrow far more
than one that is too wide, so it does not see the cost that a mixture wider by
$C + \kappa h^2 \langle\Sigma\rangle$ relative to $C$ imposes on the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance. Fitting it needs an
objective that penalizes both directions. Shrinkage also bounds $\nu$ from below, at
$2.5$ rather than $1$, since a kernel used with it must have a finite covariance.
